title: Geriatric Medication Safety & Deprescribing: Polypharmacy, Organ Function, Falls and Delirium
html:
Older adults are highly diverse. Age alone does not determine a dose, prove frailty, or justify undertreatment. Medication safety comes from matching every drug to the person’s goals, function, physiology, diagnoses, life expectancy, ability to use the regimen, and changing clinical context. The RN looks for benefit, burden, interactions, prescribing cascades, and symptoms that may actually be adverse drug effects.

Learning goals

  • Explain how age-related physiologic changes can alter drug exposure and response.
  • Complete a comprehensive medication reconciliation that includes nonprescription products.
  • Recognize anticholinergic burden, CNS polypharmacy, orthostasis, hypoglycemia, bleeding, and kidney injury.
  • Use geriatric screening tools as clinical prompts rather than automatic stop lists.
  • Identify prescribing cascades and medication-related falls or delirium.
  • Support goal-concordant, individualized deprescribing with safe tapering and follow-up.

Start with the person, not the birth date

Assess cognition, mood, hearing, vision, swallowing, dexterity, gait, falls, continence, nutrition, weight change, hydration, alcohol and substance use, kidney and liver function, blood pressure including orthostatics when indicated, living situation, caregiver support, cost, health literacy, goals, and what outcomes matter most. Ask what the person actually takes—not only what appears in the electronic record.

Medication goals may change with frailty, progressive illness, falls, or palliative priorities. A preventive medicine with a long time to benefit may no longer match the client’s goals, while symptom control may become more important. Conversely, “old age” should never be used to deny effective pain control, anticoagulation, depression treatment, vaccination, or other beneficial therapy without individualized risk–benefit assessment.

Aging can change pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics

Reduced total body water can increase concentrations of water-soluble drugs; increased body fat can prolong some lipid-soluble drugs; reduced albumin or acute illness can change protein binding. Hepatic blood flow and metabolic capacity may decline, and kidney clearance often decreases. Receptor sensitivity and homeostatic responses also change, increasing vulnerability to sedation, orthostasis, hypoglycemia, bleeding, electrolyte disturbance, and delirium.

A serum creatinine within the laboratory reference range does not guarantee normal drug clearance in a person with low muscle mass. Use the renal-function method specified in the product labeling or protocol, confirm current weight and trend, and involve pharmacy when eGFR and calculated creatinine clearance differ or the therapeutic window is narrow. “Start low and go slow” can reduce harm for selected medicines, but dosing must still reach an effective, monitored target.

A normal creatinine can hide reduced clearance
In sarcopenia, low creatinine production may make renal function look better than it is. Evaluate the whole clinical picture and the dosing method required for the exact drug.

Medication reconciliation requires a brown-bag history

Build one list containing every prescription, OTC medicine, vitamin, supplement, herb, topical product, eye or ear drop, inhaler, injection, cannabis product, and medication borrowed or saved from an old prescription. For each item record the exact product, strength, dose, route, schedule, indication, prescriber, actual use, last dose, benefit, adverse effects, and access barriers.

Compare the home list with admission, transfer, procedure, and discharge orders. Identify omissions, duplications, conflicting directions, expired therapies, brand–generic duplication, renal-dose problems, and drugs restarted despite a prior adverse effect. Include medication changes in handoff and ensure the client and caregiver know what was started, changed, continued, or stopped and why.

Polypharmacy is about appropriateness, not a number alone

Multiple medications may be necessary for multiple illnesses. Risk rises when regimens become complex, interacting, duplicative, or misaligned with goals. For every medicine ask: Is there a current indication? Is it effective? Is the dose and duration appropriate? Is it causing harm? Does another medicine treat its adverse effect? Is there a safer option? Can the person obtain and use it correctly?

A prescribing cascade occurs when a drug adverse effect is mistaken for a new disease and another drug is added. Examples include adding a diuretic for calcium-channel-blocker edema, a bladder drug for diuretic-related frequency, a cognitive enhancer for anticholinergic confusion, or a laxative without reviewing a newly constipating medication. Treat urgent symptoms, but examine the original trigger.

Beers Criteria is a screening tool, not a blacklist

The AGS Beers Criteria identifies medications that may be inappropriate in many older adults, medications to avoid with selected diseases, important interactions, drugs needing renal adjustment, and medicines associated with falls. A listed drug may still be the best option for an individual, and the criteria do not replace clinical judgment. Some recommendations do not apply in hospice or end-of-life settings.

When a medication is flagged, clarify the indication, prior alternatives, dose, duration, goals, benefit, adverse effects, and monitoring plan. Do not abruptly stop it simply because it appears on a list. Discuss safer options and document the individualized decision.

Anticholinergic burden can affect the whole person

Many first-generation antihistamines, tricyclic antidepressants, bladder antimuscarinics, antispasmodics, and other drugs contribute to cumulative anticholinergic effects. Look for dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, tachycardia, overheating, impaired accommodation, gait instability, confusion, and delirium. Risk increases when several modestly anticholinergic drugs are combined.

Diphenhydramine used as a sleep aid is a common hidden source. New confusion after an OTC product is not “normal aging.” Assess airway and vital signs, bladder and bowel function, hydration, infection, pain, hypoxia, glucose, and other causes of delirium while reviewing medication exposure.

Delirium is an emergency clue, not a normal aging change
An abrupt, fluctuating change in attention or thinking requires assessment for medications, withdrawal, infection, hypoxia, metabolic disturbance, pain, retention, constipation, stroke, and other acute causes.

CNS-active combinations increase falls and breathing risk

Benzodiazepines, sedative-hypnotics, opioids, gabapentinoids, muscle relaxants, antipsychotics, and some antidepressants can impair alertness, balance, reaction time, and ventilation. Risk rises when they are combined with each other or alcohol. Assess sedation, respiratory rate and depth, sleep apnea, gait, orthostatic symptoms, driving, cognition, and falls after initiation or dose change.

Benzodiazepines and long-term opioids can cause physical dependence; abrupt discontinuation may produce severe withdrawal. Antipsychotics carry increased mortality risk in older adults with dementia-related psychosis and are not routine sleep or behavior medicines. Before sedating a distressed client, assess pain, urinary retention, constipation, infection, unfamiliar environment, sensory loss, medication toxicity, sleep disruption, and unmet needs.

Falls require medication review and injury assessment

After a fall, first assess injury, anticoagulant exposure, neurologic status, pain, vital signs, and urgent causes. Then review new and recently changed medications, timing relative to the fall, CNS-active drugs, antihypertensives, diuretics, hypoglycemics, and medicines causing blurred vision or urgency. Measure orthostatic blood pressure when clinically appropriate and evaluate hydration, gait, footwear, vision, environment, and assistive devices.

Do not simply remove every blood-pressure or pain medicine. Identify the modifiable contributor, preserve needed therapy, adjust timing or dose when prescribed, and reassess symptoms and function. CDC STEADI recommends collaborative medication review as part of fall prevention.

Blood pressure and diuretics: evaluate standing function

Antihypertensives can prevent stroke and cardiovascular events, but excessive lowering, volume depletion, or rapid titration may cause dizziness, syncope, kidney injury, and falls. Compare supine and standing symptoms and pressures, pulse, intake, weight, edema, sodium, potassium, creatinine, and timing. Diuretics may contribute to urgency, nocturia, dehydration, hyponatremia, hypokalemia, or gout.

Acute illness, poor intake, vomiting, or diarrhea can change the safety of a stable regimen. Follow an individualized sick-day plan rather than independently stopping or continuing drugs without review.

Hypoglycemia may present atypically

Insulin and insulin secretagogues can cause prolonged or recurrent hypoglycemia, especially with kidney impairment, poor intake, weight loss, cognitive change, or mismatched meals. Older adults may present with weakness, dizziness, confusion, behavior change, fall, focal neurologic symptoms, or loss of consciousness rather than classic adrenergic signs.

Check glucose promptly with acute neurologic or functional change. Treat according to consciousness and swallowing safety, identify the medication and last meal, monitor for recurrence, and review whether the regimen and glycemic target match the client’s health status and goals.

Bleeding and kidney injury can be medication related

Anticoagulants and antiplatelets require exact indication, dose, renal function, interaction, adherence, and bleeding surveillance. A fall with head impact while anticoagulated requires prompt evaluation even without obvious external injury. Avoid assuming bruising, anemia, melena, hematuria, weakness, or confusion is an inevitable part of aging.

NSAIDs can cause GI bleeding, kidney injury, fluid retention, hypertension, and cardiovascular harm. Risk rises with dehydration, chronic kidney disease, heart failure, anticoagulants, antiplatelets, corticosteroids, and duplicate OTC NSAIDs. Assess pain alternatives and review self-treatment products.

Narrow therapeutic windows need trend-based monitoring

Digoxin, lithium, warfarin, some antiarrhythmics, antiseizure medicines, insulin, and other high-risk drugs require drug-specific surveillance. Kidney decline, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance, acute illness, interacting antibiotics, or a new supplement may make a previously stable dose toxic. Verify laboratory timing and assess the client rather than reacting to a number alone.

New anorexia, nausea, weakness, confusion, tremor, ataxia, vision change, bradycardia, bleeding, or dysrhythmia may be toxicity. Hold and escalate according to the medication, severity, prescription, and protocol.

Deprescribing is a monitored clinical intervention

Deprescribing is the planned reduction or discontinuation of a medicine when harms, burden, or lack of benefit outweigh likely benefit in the context of the client’s goals. It is not abandonment or indiscriminate pill reduction. Include the client, caregiver when authorized, prescriber, pharmacist, and relevant specialists.

  1. Reconcile the actual regimen and identify the indication for each medicine.
  2. Prioritize drugs causing current harm, without benefit, duplicative, or inconsistent with goals.
  3. Check whether withdrawal, rebound, or disease recurrence requires a taper.
  4. Agree on one clear change, monitoring plan, rescue plan, and follow-up interval.
  5. Document and communicate the change to every care setting and pharmacy.

Benzodiazepines, beta blockers, clonidine, corticosteroids, antiseizure medicines, antidepressants, and long-term opioids are examples that may require individualized tapering. Do not stop them abruptly unless a specific emergency plan requires it. Monitor symptom recurrence, withdrawal, blood pressure, pulse, mood, sleep, pain, function, and quality of life.

Stopping a medicine can cause harm too
A safe deprescribing plan names what is changing, how quickly, what to monitor, whom to call, and what would trigger pausing or reversing the taper.

Make the regimen usable

Assess bottle opening, pill size, swallowing, vision, hearing, language, numeracy, memory, dexterity, schedule complexity, food requirements, cost, transportation, and pharmacy access. Simplify timing and formulations when clinically possible. Use large-print instructions, accessible packaging, blister packs or organizers when appropriate, alarms, and one updated medication list.

Teach-back should include purpose, exact dose and time, special administration, missed-dose action, important interactions, urgent adverse effects, storage, and who manages refills. Confirm the plan with the person who actually prepares the medication while preserving the older adult’s autonomy and consent.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Identify the complete regimen, indications, actual use, recent changes, cognition, falls, orthostasis, organ function, hydration, nutrition, alcohol, adherence barriers, adverse effects, and client goals.
  2. Analyze cues: Distinguish disease progression, undertreatment, drug toxicity, interaction, withdrawal, duplicate therapy, prescribing cascade, delirium, hypoglycemia, bleeding, or renal accumulation.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Respiratory depression, anaphylaxis, severe hypoglycemia, intracranial bleeding, dangerous dysrhythmia, withdrawal seizure, shock, and acute delirium require urgent action.
  4. Generate solutions: Stabilize the client, hold harmful exposure when appropriate, check glucose and targeted studies, reconcile medicines, consult pharmacy, reduce fall hazards, and create a goal-concordant adjustment or taper.
  5. Take action: Administer the verified regimen safely, communicate changes across transitions, teach with accessible tools, and activate emergency care for instability.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Reassess symptoms, function, cognition, gait, falls, blood pressure, glucose, bleeding, organ function, withdrawal, adherence, burden, and the client’s own goals.

Clinical example

An older adult develops acute confusion, dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation, and an unsteady gait after starting an OTC nighttime product containing diphenhydramine. The RN recognizes a possible anticholinergic syndrome rather than assuming dementia progression, assesses vital signs, glucose, oxygenation, bladder volume, bowel status, infection and other delirium causes, holds further exposure, and notifies the clinical team. After stabilization, the RN and pharmacist review the entire medication list and create a safer sleep plan.

Original educational synthesis. Medication selection, dosing, renal calculations, monitoring, deprescribing, tapering, and emergency response require current prescriptions, product labeling, individualized goals, local policy, pharmacist and prescriber review, and qualified clinical supervision. Geriatric screening criteria support but do not replace clinical judgment. This lesson is not medical advice, clinical decision support, continuing education, or an official AGS or NCSBN product.
